{{Short description|Mathematical concept}}

{{Confusing|date=May 2026}}

'''K-convexity in Rn''' is a mathematical concept.

==Formula==
Let ''<math>\Kappa</math>''= (''K<sub>0</sub>'',''K<sub>1</sub>'',...,''K<sub>n</sub>'') to be a vector of (n+1) nonnegative constants and define a function <math>\Kappa</math>(<sup>.</sup>): <math>\Re_+^n</math>  → <math>\Re_+^1</math> as follows:

<math>\Kappa</math>(<math>x</math>) = ''K<sub>0</sub>''<math>\delta</math>(''e''<math>x</math>) + <math>\sum_{i=1}^n</math>''K<sub>i</sub>''<math>\delta</math>(<math>x_i</math>),

where ''e'' = (1,1,...,1) ∈ <math>\Re^n</math>, <math>\Re_+^n = \{x \in \Re^n | x \geq 0 \}</math>, <math>\delta</math>(0) = 0 and <math>\delta(z)</math>= 1 for all <math>z</math> > 0.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal
| last1=Gallego | first1=G.
| last2=Sethi | first2=S. P.
| date=2005
| url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/257604732_K-Convexity_in_Rn
| title=<math>\mathcal{K}</math>-convexity in <math>\mathfrak{R}^n</math>
| journal=Journal of Optimization Theory & Applications
| volume=127
| issue=1
| pages=71–88
| doi=10.1007/s10957-005-6393-4}}</ref>

The concept of '''K'''-convexity generalizes ''K''[[K-convex function|-convexity]] introduced by [[Herbert Scarf|Scarf]] (1960)<ref>{{cite report
| last1=Scarf | first1=Herbert
| date=1960
| title=The Optimality of (S, s) Policies in the Dynamic Inventory Problem
| publisher=Stanford, CA: Stanford University Press
| url=https://purl.stanford.edu/bt748ps8245}}</ref> to higher dimensional spaces and is useful in multiproduct inventory problems with fixed setup costs. Scarf used ''K''[[K-convex function|-convexity]] to prove the optimality of the (s, S) policy in the single product case. Several papers are devoted to obtaining optimal policies for multiple product problems with fixed ordering costs.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{cite journal

This definition introduced by Gallego and [[Suresh P. Sethi|Sethi]] (2005)<ref name=":0" /> is motivated by the joint replenishment problem when we incur a setup cost ''K<sub>0</sub>'', whenever we order an item or items and an individual setup cost ''K<sub>i</sub>'' for each item <math>i</math> we order. There are some important special cases:

(i) The simplest is the case of one product or ''n'' = 1, where  ''K<sub>0</sub> + K<sub>1</sub>'' can be considered to be the setup cost.  

(ii) The joint setup cost arises when ''K<sub>i</sub>'' = 0'', <math>i</math>'' = 1'','' 2'', . . . , n,'' and a setup cost of <math>\Kappa_0</math> is incurred whenever any one or more of the items are ordered.  In this case,  ''<math>\Kappa</math>'' = ''(K<sub>0</sub>,'' 0'','' 0'', . . . ,'' 0'')'' and  <math>\Kappa</math>(<math>x</math>) = ''K<sub>0</sub><math>\delta</math>''(''e''<math>x</math>).

(iii) When there is no joint setup cost, i.e., ''K<sub>0</sub>''  = 0, and there are only individual setups, we have ''<math>\Kappa</math>(<math>x</math>)'' = <math>\sum_{i=1}^n</math>''K<sub>i</sub>''<math>\delta</math>(<math>x_i</math>)''.''
